{{short description|American mathematician}}

'''Dudley Weldon Woodard''' (October 3, 1881 – July 1, 1965) was a Galveston-born American mathematician and professor, and the second [[African-American]] to earn a PhD in mathematics; the first was Woodard's mentor [[Elbert Frank Cox]], who earned a PhD from [[Cornell]] in 1925.

He received his B.A. degree from [[Wilberforce University]] in Ohio (1903), his B.S. degree (1906) and M.Sc. degree (1907) at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="archives.upenn">[http://www.archives.upenn.edu/histy/features/aframer/math.html Pioneer African American Mathematicians, University of Pennsylvania University Archives], archives.upenn.edu; accessed July 9, 2020.</ref> He taught collegiate mathematics in Tuskegee for many years,<ref name="Chesnutt2002">{{cite book|author=Charles Waddell Chesnutt|title=An Exemplary Citizen: Letters of Charles W. Chesnutt, 1906-1932|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xzfRwYBm3ScC&pg=PA42|year=2002|publisher=Stanford University Press|isbn=978-0-8047-4508-6|pages=42–}}</ref> until finally he earned his PhD at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] (1928).<ref name="FarmerShepherd-Wynn2012">{{cite book|author1=Vernon L. Farmer|author2=Evelyn Shepherd-Wynn|title=Voices of Historical and Contemporary Black American Pioneers &#91;4 volumes&#93;|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O8tEwW7E8PIC&pg=PA33|date=15 May 2012|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-0-313-39225-2|pages=33–}}</ref> His doctoral thesis was entitled, ''On Two-Dimensional Analysis Situs with Special Reference to the Jordan Curve Theorem'', and was advised by [[John Robert Kline|John R. Kline]].<ref name="math.buffalo">[http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/woodard_dudleyw.html Dudley W. Woodard, Mathematician of the African Diaspora], math.buffalo.edu; accessed July 9, 2020.</ref><ref name="GuzmanFoster1947">{{cite book|author1=Jessie Parkhurst Guzman|author2=Vera Chandler Foster|author3=William Hardin Hughes|title=Negro year book: a review of events affecting Negro life, 1941-1946|url=https://archive.org/details/negroyearbookrev00guzmrich|year=1947|publisher=Dept. of Records and Research, Tuskegee Institute|access-date=July 9, 2020}}</ref>

During his lifetime, he published three papers. The second of these, ''The Characterization of the Closed N-Cell'' in [[Fundamenta Mathematicae]], 13 (1929), is, according to Scott Williams, Professor of Mathematics at the [[State University of New York-Buffalo]], the first paper published in an accredited mathematics journal by an African American.<ref name="math.buffalo"/><ref name="February22">[https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1922-28-05/S0002-9904-1922-03534-3/S0002-9904-1922-03534-3.pdf "February 1922 Meeting"]. ''American Mathematical Society''.</ref> He also published a study for the Committee of twelve for the advancement of the interests of the Negro race on [[Jackson, Mississippi]] in 1909,<ref name="Negro progress Jackson">{{cite book|last1=Woodard|first1=Dudley Weldon|title=Negro progress in a Mississippi town, being a study of conditions in Jackson, Mississippi|date=1909|publisher=Committee of twelve for the advancement of the interests of the Negro race|location=Cheyney, Pa|url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/100640898|access-date=8 April 2017}}</ref> a textbook, ''Practical Arithmetic'' (1911),<ref name="Practical Arithmetic">{{cite book|last1=Woodard|first1=Dudley Weldon|title=Practical Arithmetic|date=1911|publisher=Tuskegee Normal & Industrial Institute|url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/100657866|access-date=8 April 2017}}</ref> and an article on geometry teaching at Tuskegee in 1913.<ref name="Geometry">{{cite journal|last1=Woodard|first1=D. W.|title=The Teaching of Geometry at Tuskegee|journal=School Science and Mathematics|date=May 1913|volume=13|issue=5|pages=400–410|doi=10.1111/j.1949-8594.1913.tb07751.x|hdl=2027/emu.010000894067|s2cid=122604204 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Woodard was a respected mathematician, professor and mentor to his students at [[Howard University]] in Washington DC, where he established the masters program in mathematics.<ref name="Walker2014">{{cite book|author=Erica N. Walker|title=Beyond Banneker: Black Mathematicians and the Paths to Excellence|url=https://archive.org/details/beyondbannekerbl0000walk|url-access=registration|date=29 May 2014|publisher=SUNY Press|isbn=978-1-4384-5215-9|pages=[https://archive.org/details/beyondbannekerbl0000walk/page/115 115]–}}</ref> One of his best known students was [[William Waldron Schieffelin Claytor]], who later took his PhD at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] (1933), also under Woodard's former advisor, [[John R. Kline]].

Woodard retired in 1947, after having become chairman of the mathematics department. He died on July 15, 1965, at his home in [[Cleveland, Ohio]], aged 83.<ref name="archives.upenn" /><ref name="Dean1997">{{cite book|author=Nathaniel Dean|title=African Americans in Mathematics: DIMACS Workshop, June 26-28, 1996|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ugnntzZ0a_kC&pg=PA186|date=1 January 1997|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-7079-2|pages=186–}}</ref><ref name="Newell1980">{{cite book|author=Virginia K. Newell|title=Black Mathematicians and Their Works|title-link=Black Mathematicians and Their Works|date=June 1980|publisher=Dorrance|isbn=978-0-8059-2556-2}}</ref><ref name="PalmerCulture2006">{{cite book|author1=Colin A. Palmer|author2=Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture|title=Encyclopedia of African-American culture and history: the Black experience in the Americas|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cS0OAQAAMAAJ|year=2006|publisher=Macmillan Reference USA|isbn=978-0-02-865820-9}}</ref><ref>[http://www.myblackhistory.net/Dudley_Woodard.htm Black Scientists in America: Dudley Weldon Woodard], myblackhistory.net; accessed July 9, 2020.</ref>
